posts.quote: DAD SWAPPED THE STORM WINDOWS FOR SCREENS EVERY APRIL, AND THE WHOLE HOUSE FINALLY EXHALED.
posts.caption: Every window frame on the house had a number penciled into the corner, and every storm window had the matching number so it could find its way home. Dad climbed the ladder one April Saturday and handed them down to me like they were made of glass. They went up into the garage rafters wrapped in old bedsheets, and the screens came out smelling like dust and last summer. By supper the curtains were moving for the first time since October. Mom stood in the kitchen with her eyes closed for a minute and didn't say a word. That was how we knew winter was officially over.
posts.first: Our window numbers were in Dad's square carpenter's handwriting, and they're still on the frames if you look close. I held the ladder every year and never got thanked until the last window was in. Then he'd say "good help," and that was a paycheck.

posts.quote: THE MAILBOX ON THE CORNER HAD A TIN PLATE WITH THE PICKUP TIMES, AND THE MAIL TRUCK WAS NEVER LATE.
posts.caption: A letter written at the kitchen table on Sunday night went into that box by Monday morning, and you could say with a straight face that it would be in Ohio by Thursday. Mom checked the little plate for the last pickup before she'd lick the stamp, because a letter that missed the truck missed the whole day. The mail carrier walked his route in a gray uniform and shorts in July, and he knew which houses had a dog. You dropped the envelope through the slot, pulled the handle once to make sure, and heard it land on top of everybody else's news. It felt like the whole country was running on a clock you could trust.
posts.first: My grandmother wrote me every other week and always numbered the page corners in case they came out of order. I never saw her miss the last pickup. Her letters came in the same blue ink with the same sentence about the weather.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the egg man)
posts.quote: THE EGG MAN / A WIRE BASKET, A DOZEN BROWN EGGS, AND A KNOCK AT THE BACK DOOR
posts.caption: He came every Thursday morning, a little after the dishes were done. He knocked at the back door, because only strangers used the front. Mom took the eggs, held a couple up to the window like she was checking a diamond, and paid him in coins counted out of a jar. The carton went on the counter and the shells went in the garden, and nothing was wasted at that house. The yolks were so orange you could see the difference on a plate of toast. I have never found one like them since.
posts.first: Our egg man was Mr. Dietz, and he always left a feather on top of the carton, I think just to make us smile. He and Mom talked about the weather for ten minutes every week like it was a business meeting. When he stopped coming, she kept the wire basket on top of the refrigerator for years.

posts.quote: THE CHURCH PAGEANT HAD BATHROBE SHEPHERDS AND TINSEL ANGELS, AND THE BEST PART WAS THE KID WHO FORGOT HIS LINE.
posts.caption: Rehearsals started the Sunday after Thanksgiving, and the costumes came out of the same cardboard box every year. The bathrobes were always a size too big, and the towels slid down over one eye the second you turned your head. The angels had wings made of coat hangers wrapped in tinsel that shed on everything. When your line came you stood there, and the whole basement got quiet enough to hear the furnace. A kid in the front row mouthed it for you until it came loose. Nobody remembers which year it went perfectly, but everybody remembers the shepherd who said hello to the audience.
posts.first: I was a shepherd three years running because I could carry the staff without hitting anybody. One year my mother sewed a gold ribbon on my towel, and I felt like a movie star. I still remember how it felt to wear it.

posts.quote: The good scissors lived in the sewing basket, and everyone in the house knew not to cut paper with them.
posts.first: Ours had green handles and lived under the spool of white thread. My mother could tell from across the room if somebody had cut paper with them. She never raised her voice about it, but the whole house understood.

posts.quote: A COFFEE CAN OF BACON GREASE SAT BY THE STOVE, AND IT FLAVORED EVERYTHING FROM GREEN BEANS TO PIE CRUST.
posts.caption: Nobody threw out the drippings. Mom poured them through a square of cloth into an old coffee can and set it back on the stove, where it stayed solid all winter. A spoonful went into the green beans, another into the biscuits, and a third into the skillet before the cornbread. The kitchen smelled like Sunday on a Tuesday. She'd have called it frugal, but the way those beans tasted, it was closer to a secret ingredient. Every cook in the family kept a can like it, and none of them would tell you how old the grease was.
posts.first: Grandma's can was blue enamel with a chip on the lid, and it never seemed to run out. I asked her once what she put in her green beans and she said, "Love and a spoonful." It was bacon grease, and she knew I knew.

posts.quote: DAD ALWAYS BACKED INTO THE DRIVEWAY, AND IN FORTY YEARS HE NEVER ONCE SAID WHY.
posts.caption: He'd pull past the house, stop, shift into reverse, and swing that big sedan around with one arm over the seat. It took him less than ten seconds, and he never once clipped the mailbox. Mom said it was so he could leave in a hurry. Dad said it was so the headlights faced the road. I figured out as a grown man that he was just ready, for anything, at any hour. The car sat there every night nose out and the keys hung on the hook, like a man with his boots by the bed.
posts.first: I back into my own driveway now, and I still couldn't tell you why. My wife quit mentioning it years ago. Somewhere, Dad is nodding.

posts.quote: THE CLASS ATLAS / A HEAVY BOOK, A FINGER ON THE MAP, AND A TOWN YOU WOULD NEVER VISIT
posts.caption: The atlas lived on the shelf under the window and weighed more than your lunch box and your coat together. When Mrs. Halvorsen let you carry it to your desk, you felt chosen. You opened it to a page of tiny printed names and found a river that ran through three countries you couldn't pronounce. A finger followed the red road from one city to the next, and for ten minutes you were traveling. None of us went to most of those places. We just liked knowing they were there, and that somebody had drawn the way.
posts.first: I picked the same page every time, a coastline in the far north with names I couldn't say. Years later I found out I'd been mispronouncing every one of them, and I'm not sorry. That book told me the world was bigger than our town.

posts.character: Entertainment (the ball game in the garage)
posts.quote: GRANDPA LISTENED TO THE BALL GAME IN THE GARAGE, AND YOU WERE WELCOME AS LONG AS YOU STAYED QUIET.
posts.caption: The radio sat on the workbench between a cigar box of nails and a jar of washers, and the volume was set so low you had to lean in. Grandpa never said a word between pitches. Sometimes he'd nod once, and that meant something had happened that we both understood. I learned the batting order from a man who only spoke when somebody got on base. When the game ended he switched the radio off, folded his lawn chair, and said, "Well." That was the whole conversation, and I'd give a lot to have it again.
posts.first: He kept score on the back of an old envelope with the stub of a pencil, and I found a stack of those envelopes after he was gone. Every one has the date written in the corner. I keep them in my desk drawer.

posts.character: Home life (the water bucket and dipper)
posts.quote: THE WATER BUCKET AND TIN DIPPER STOOD BY THE KITCHEN DOOR, AND THE FIRST SIP WAS ALWAYS THE COLDEST.
posts.caption: Before the kitchen got a faucet that ran cold, there was a bucket by the back door. Somebody carried it full from the pump every morning, and a tin dipper hung from the rim by its hook. You came in from the field with dust on your tongue and took the first long drink without stopping. The water tasted a little like the metal and a lot like relief. Grandfather drank from the dipper standing up, wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, and hung it back exactly where it belonged.
posts.first: My grandmother scrubbed that bucket every Saturday with sand and a brush. The dipper had a dent in the handle from some long-ago drop that nobody could remember. I have it on a shelf now, and I wouldn't dare put water in it.
